3.2.5.3-r1.burton_quote: For what’s an whore, as he saith, but a poller of youth, ruin of men, a destruction, a devourer of patrimonies, a downfall of honour, fodder for the devil, the gate of death, and supplement of hell

3.2.5.3-r10.burton_quote: massy plate of silver, gold, enamelled, beset with jewels, golden candlesticks, goodly rich hangings, brave furniture, heard his trumpets sound, Fifes, Drums, and his exquisite music in all kinds: when they had observed his majestical presence as he sat in purple robes, crowned with his sceptre, &c., in his royal seat

3.2.5.3-r12.burton_quote: they had been much better to have been childless

3.2.5.3-r13.burton_quote: that he was unchaste, because his wife Adelaide the daughter of Henry Landgrave of Hassia, was so deformed
3.2.5.3-r13.translation: he had his way with the maidservants

3.2.5.3-r16.burton_quote: for why was Daphne turned into a green bay-tree, but to show that virginity is immortal
3.2.5.3-r16.translation: immortal glory is prepared for virgins who keep their chastity

3.2.5.3-r2.burton_quote: what I am without, but within God knows

3.2.5.3-r4.burton_quote: and after he had used her as a wife one night, because her breath stunk, they say, or for some other secret fault, sent her back again to her father
3.2.5.3-r4.translation: it is uncertain why he took offence; … doing a thing plainly unlawful, and most unbecoming to a royal person

3.2.5.3-r5.burton_quote: as mutable as a flower, and ’tis not nature so makes us, but most part the infirmity of the beholder

3.2.5.3-r6.burton_quote: When thou seest a fair and beautiful person, a brave Bona-roba, a bella Donna, quae salivam moveat, lepidam puellam & quam tu facile ames, a comely woman, having bright eyes, a merry countenance, a shining lustre in her look, a pleasant grace, wringing thy soul, and increasing thy concupiscence; bethink with thyself that it is but earth thou lovest, a mere excrement, which so vexeth thee, which thou so admirest
3.2.5.3-r6.translation: think of her already growing old, wrinkled, hollow-cheeked, sick; she is full within of such filth, phlegm and dung; consider what she carries within her nostrils, eyes and brain, what filth, etc.

3.2.5.3-r9.burton_quote: a wife is a fever hectic, as Scaliger calls her, and not to be cured but by death
